standard.title: Identify patterns and relationships
standard.description: evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, or to infer relationships
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS5S03 (Evaluate patterns and trends): Students can identify patterns and trends in information and data across a range of formats, and infer relationships. Students can read and analyse multiple graph types.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, and infer cause-effect relationships, including across historical, geographic and social domains.

nodes.label: Causes, effects and significance in historical data
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine sources to identify the causes, effects and significance of past events and developments, using evidence to support their analysis.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the causes and effects of one past event or development using at least one source.
nodes.typical_width: Examine sources to identify causes, effects and significance of past events and developments — such as the Wave Hill walk-off, Wik decision, health policies and migration policies — and explain how these events have brought about change.
wider: Analyse the causes, effects and significance of two related events and assess how one contributed to the other (causal chain analysis)
Investigate how different historians have assessed the significance of the same event — and explain why significance assessments may differ
nodes.hinge_reason: The move to cause-effect-significance analysis is more demanding than Year 5 pattern identification — students who cannot systematically identify causes AND effects AND significance will reduce complex historical analysis to simple description.

response_modes.reason: Use an explicit causes/effects/significance framework applied to a worked example before students apply it independently. The three-part structure requires deliberate scaffolding.

success_criteria: Students identify at least one cause, one effect and one indicator of significance for a past event.
Students support each component with reference to source evidence.

nodes.label: Identifying patterns using graphic organisers and maps
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use graphic organisers, maps and concept maps to identify patterns, trends and cause-effect relationships in HASS data.
nodes.minimum_width: Use one graphic organiser or map to identify a pattern, trend or relationship in HASS data.
nodes.typical_width: Use graphic organisers (maps, concept maps, tables, charts) to identify patterns — such as settlement in regional agricultural areas — trends (e.g. changes in Australian immigration statistics) and cause-effect relationships (e.g. war and refugee movement, consumer decisions and environmental sustainability).
wider: Create a concept map that traces the system of causes and effects for a complex Year 6 topic (e.g. how consumer decisions affect environment and community), identifying second and third-order effects
Analyse Australian immigration statistics across multiple decades using a graph, identifying trends and proposing explanations for each change observed

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from using multiple graphic tools across different topics — each tool reveals different features of the data. Build a repertoire of analytical tools rather than deepening expertise in one.

success_criteria: Students use a graphic organiser or map to identify a pattern, trend or relationship.
Students describe what the pattern, trend or relationship shows about the HASS topic.

nodes.label: Evaluating past attitudes and proposing reasons for change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate attitudes and actions of the past that seem strange or unacceptable by contemporary standards, and propose reasons why values and social norms change over time.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one past attitude or practice that is no longer acceptable and propose one reason why values changed.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate attitudes and actions of the past that now seem unacceptable (e.g. deportation of South Sea Islanders, denial of voting rights, institutional child care practices), propose reasons why these were accepted at the time and why values changed; reflect on what aspects of current society might be viewed similarly in the future.
wider: Investigate a specific historical shift in social values (e.g. attitudes toward immigration, gender equality) and trace the events, movements and arguments that drove the change
Reflect on a current issue and propose which aspects of contemporary society might be judged negatively by future generations — and what this suggests about the nature of social progress

response_modes.reason: Evaluating past attitudes requires students to hold two temporal frames simultaneously (past context and present standards) — scaffold explicitly by asking students to explain both what was accepted then and why it is not now.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Reflecting on future judgments of current practices is a sophisticated and generative thinking move — connecting historical pattern analysis to futures thinking with genuine civic and ethical implications.
success_criteria: Students identify at least one past attitude or practice that is no longer considered acceptable.
Students explain why it was accepted at the time and why values have changed.

nodes.label: Evaluating data to identify patterns and infer relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate information and data from multiple formats to identify patterns and trends, and infer cause-effect relationships, using evidence to support their analysis.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a pattern or trend and infer a cause-effect relationship from information in at least two formats.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate information and data from a range of formats (maps, charts, written sources, graphic organisers, historical sources) to identify patterns, trends and cause-effect relationships across Year 6 HASS topics; support inferences with evidence; acknowledge where evidence is ambiguous or incomplete.
wider: Evaluate competing explanations for a historical pattern and assess which has stronger evidential support
Propose reasons why socially sustainable practices (negotiation, arbitration, reconciliation, cultural mediation) resolve issues peacefully — drawing on patterns identified from historical examples

response_modes.reason: Integrated pattern analysis across formats and topics requires students to bring together data literacy, historical thinking and cause-effect reasoning. Support with a structured analysis protocol.

success_criteria: Students identify at least one pattern and infer at least one cause-effect relationship from evidence.
Students support their analysis with reference to at least two sources or data formats.
Students acknowledge ambiguity or limitations in the evidence where appropriate.
